extracted.intended_audience: health-psychology researchers, meta-analysts, and clinicians interested in well-being–health evidence
extracted.subtask_description: A systematic meta-analysis synthesizing empirical studies that measure or manipulate positive psychological constructs (well-being) and report objective physical health outcomes, including moderator coding and effect-size aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search strategy (three-pronged)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine prior reviews (identify empirical articles cited by two recent reviews), forward and backward citation searching from that set, and an independent database search (PsycINFO and Web of Science) to locate additional studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start from the empirical articles included in key prior reviews (here, 240 unique empirical articles), locate reviews/theoretical articles cited by them (additional titles), then perform backward (reference lists) and forward (citing articles) searches. Finally run a database search combining predefined well-being and health search terms to capture missed studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Database search term set
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine multiple synonyms for well-being and multiple descriptors of health in database searches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example used: five well-being terms (positive affect, subjective well-being, happiness, life satisfaction, hedonic quality of life) combined with three health terms (physical health, physical well-being, physical functioning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Search time frame
rubrics_metrics.description: Include studies published or posted through a specified cut-off date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This meta-analysis included all potentially relevant studies published or posted through June 1, 2006; set and report a clear cut-off for inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion criterion: language
rubrics_metrics.description: Study must be written in English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude non-English reports unless translated or otherwise accessible in English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion criterion: empirical study
rubrics_metrics.description: Study must be empirical (not a literature review, meta-analysis, or theoretical paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only primary data reports were eligible for effect-size computation and coding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion criterion: independent variable is well-being
rubrics_metrics.description: Study must include a subjective measure of well-being (e.g., positive affect, life satisfaction, happiness, optimism) or a manipulation of positive mood/emotion (e.g., humorous films, imagining pleasant circumstances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include both trait and state measures/manipulations of positive constructs; record the exact construct for coding (see state vs trait rubric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion criterion: dependent variable is objective physical health
rubrics_metrics.description: Study must include an objective measure of physical health (e.g., mortality/survival, respiratory functioning, endocrine and immune functioning, pain tolerance, disease progression, heart disease, cancer, HIV symptoms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-report-only health measures are not sufficient; provide concrete biomedical or physiological markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion criterion: sample group specified
rubrics_metrics.description: Study must state the specific sample group (e.g., cancer patients, healthy students, asthmatics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear description of the population/sample is required for moderator coding (health status, age, gender composition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion criterion: allowable study designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Study must use experimental, ambulatory, or longitudinal methodology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-sectional/correlational studies that cannot address directionality were excluded; these three designs were required to examine prospective or causal relations between well-being and objective health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement: effect size must be provided or computable
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect size between well-being and health must either be reported or be computable from summary, descriptive, or inferential statistics (t, F, odds ratios, Chi-square, exact p-values).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When only regression or probit analyses are reported, compute r-equivalent effect sizes using methods such as Rosenthal & Rubin (2003) from exact p-values or use conservative p cut-offs if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: ill-being-only studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies that measured or manipulated only ill-being constructs (e.g., depression, hostility, negative affect, anger).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The focus is on positive psychological constructs; studies must include well-being (or both well-being and ill-being) to be eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: contemporaneous-only correlations
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies that assess only contemporaneous (cross-sectional) correlations between well-being and health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such designs provide little information regarding directionality and were not eligible for this meta-analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: cross-sectional mean-difference-only studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies that examined only cross-sectional mean differences between healthy and unhealthy samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies must allow inference about the effect of well-being on health (prospective, experimental, or ambulatory designs), not merely group differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: self-report health-only measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies that measure health using only self-report measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective biomedical or physiological markers are required to reduce shared method variance and better assess tangible health impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: reverse-direction studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies that examine the impact of physical health on well-being rather than the effect of well-being on health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The meta-analysis focuses on well-being as predictor and physical health as outcome; reverse-direction studies do not meet this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of analysis: independent samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat each independent sample within a study as the primary unit of analysis; calculate effect sizes for each independent sample and each outcome measured/manipulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a study reports separate statistics for subgroups (e.g., males vs females, healthy vs unhealthy), compute separate effect sizes; for aggregated central tendency and homogeneity tests, aggregate multiple effect sizes to derive one r per independent sample so each sample contributes only one r to those analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect size metric: correlation coefficient (r)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the correlation coefficient (r index) as the primary effect-size metric for relations between well-being and health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effect sizes computed with Comprehensive Meta-Analysis 2.0 (Borenstein et al., 2005). For experiments comparing groups, compute appropriate r or transform reported statistics to r.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect-size computation rules for multi-condition designs
rubrics_metrics.description: When studies induce both positive and negative affect, compute separate effect sizes for positive-affect→health and negative-affect→health; when studies compare difference scores between positive and negative mood manipulation groups, compute a single effect size estimating the differential impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about what each computed r represents (positive-affect effect, negative-affect effect, or differential effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of sign and direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive r values indicate relations in the predicted direction (well-being enhancing health outcomes); negative r values indicate relations opposite to predictions (well-being associated with compromised outcomes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistently apply sign conventions when entering effect sizes; report predicted direction hypotheses and interpret accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective health outcome coding taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Code objective health outcomes into three general categories (short-term, long-term, chronic conditions) and multiple specific variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short-term (molecular-level) outcomes: immune system response (e.g., sIgA, NKCA), endocrine response (cortisol, epinephrine, norepinephrine), cardiovascular reactivity (blood pressure, heart rate), physiological response (finger temperature, skin conductance), pain tolerance (cold pressor time). Long-term (molar-level for normal functioning): general health (e.g., mucus weight, cholesterol), cardiovascular functioning (HRV, ischemic episodes), respiratory functioning (inspiratory volume), longevity. Chronic-condition outcomes: respiratory diseases/conditions (FEV, bronchial responsiveness), disease progression (viral load, recovery), survival.

rubrics_metrics.name: State vs trait coding for well-being constructs
rubrics_metrics.description: Record the exact subjective well-being construct and code it as a state variable (momentary positive/negative affect, induced hope, relaxation) or a trait variable (global life satisfaction, happiness, optimism, trait affect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classification enables moderator analyses comparing momentary versus dispositional effects on objective health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample characteristic coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Code sample-level moderators including study method (experimental, ambulatory, longitudinal), baseline health status of the sample (healthy vs unhealthy), mean participant age, and gender composition (percent male).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extract coding information from the Methods section of each article; these moderators are used in categorical comparisons and meta-regressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fixed vs random effects models
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute aggregate effect sizes with both fixed and random effects models; focus on random-effects results for generalizability but use fixed-effects where required (e.g., certain moderator tests).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Random-effects models allow broader generalization and partition between- and within-study variance; fixed-effects models provide more precise estimates and are required for some meta-regression or certain post-hoc tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation and weighting under fixed effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When using fixed-effects models, calculate central tendency by averaging weighted r effect sizes using inverse-variance weights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both fixed and random results, and specify weighting procedures used for fixed-effect aggregates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogeneity testing and moderator analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use homogeneity tests (Q statistics) to assess whether variance in effect sizes is explained by proposed moderators. For categorical moderators, use QBET to test between-group heterogeneity; if significant (p < 0.05), perform post-hoc contrasts to identify group differences. For continuous moderators, use meta-regression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report Qw (within-group) and QBET (between-group) values and p-values; choose fixed vs random appropriately for each test and follow Hedges (1994) steps for post-hoc contrasts under fixed effects as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling non-independence of multiple outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not statistically compare average effect sizes across different health outcomes when many independent samples measure multiple, non-independent outcomes; instead compare effect sizes within each health-outcome category to determine significance relative to zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because effect sizes from the same sample for different outcomes are not independent, avoid direct cross-outcome statistical comparisons unless independence is established or appropriate multilevel methods are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Base sample and variable coding decisions on information reported in the Methods section of each article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document coding choices and any assumptions; report frequency distributions of coded moderators (e.g., % experimental designs, publication years, funding sources, country).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predicted directional hypotheses for specific outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: State a priori expectations about which health outcomes well-being should improve or reduce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples here: expect well-being to increase health-related functioning, cardiovascular functioning, and immune response; expect well-being to decrease cardiovascular reactivity, endocrine response, physiological response, symptom response in chronic conditions, and disease progression. Use these predictions to interpret aggregated effect sizes.
